fixes.explanation: The fortieth year it is, friend. The writer says, "In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month, Moses proclaimed to the Israelites all that the LORD had commanded him concerning them." (Deuteronomy 1:3). Even the day is on the calendar. Forty years, and somebody kept count.

Second year is a fair guess, but the text says fortieth. The writer says, "In the fortieth year, on the first day of the eleventh month…" (Deuteronomy 1:3). Forty is a big number. My longest wait in a drawer never came with a date that exact.

Explain is the word, baker. In the land of Moab, "Moses began to explain this law…" (Deuteronomy 1:5). Not a new law and not a rewrite. He starts walking them through it, and I tell you, I have stood over a recipe card and explained it to a mixing bowl, so I respect the effort.

Shorten sounds tidy, baker, but the text says Moses "began to explain this law…" (Deuteronomy 1:5). Explaining and shortening are two different jobs. He's helping them understand it, not trimming it down to fit on a sticky note.

No lots here, baker. Moses says, "Choose for yourselves wise, understanding, and respected men from each of your tribes…" (Deuteronomy 1:13). Notice he asks for men, plural, from every tribe. One new leader would just be Moses with a different hat, and I know a thing or two about wearing one tall hat and still being buried in work.

Twelve leaders sounds tidy, but that's not what the text says. Moses appoints them "as commanders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens, and as officers for your tribes." (Deuteronomy 1:15). The verse gives four sizes of command, and no number like twelve. Count the groups in the verse, friend, and you land on four.

God, baker! Moses tells the judges, "Do not be intimidated by anyone, for judgment belongs to God." (Deuteronomy 1:17). Think about that. The big person in front of you is not the one holding the final say. That's why they can hear small and great alike without shaking in their sandals.

Careful, friend, that one's true. Moses says, "And bring to me any case too difficult for you, and I will hear it." (Deuteronomy 1:17). The judges don't have to sweat the hard ones alone. There's a place to carry them, and every one of us has stared at a problem too big and wished for that.
